title: Lucknow's Melt-in-Your-Mouth Moment: How the City of Nawabs Became a UNESCO Culinary Capital
excerpt: With a CNN spotlight and a UNESCO designation, Lucknow's centuries-old Awadhi cuisine is finally being recognized on the global stage — a bittersweet vindication for NRIs who always knew.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Lucknow is now a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy, recognizing its rich culinary heritage.
  • It is the second Indian city to receive this designation, following Hyderabad in 2019.
  • Awadhi cuisine emphasizes subtlety and technique, contrasting with the heavier Mughlai style.
  • The city's vegetarian dishes and street food are integral to its culinary identity.
  • Lucknow's recognition boosts global interest in diverse Indian culinary traditions.
Lucknow's Culinary Recognition
›UNESCO designation announced in October 2025.
›Second Indian city recognized, after Hyderabad in 2019.
›Over 400 cities globally are part of the culinary network.
›Recognition highlights deep-rooted culinary traditions.
Every NRI who has ever tried to explain galawati kebabs to a friend at a dinner party — the melt-on-your-tongue texture, the 160-spice secret blend, the fact that they were invented for a toothless king — has long known what the rest of the world is only now discovering. Lucknow, the unhurried capital of Uttar Pradesh and the historic seat of the Nawabs of Awadh, has been named a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy. And this week, CNN Travel gave the designation its biggest international amplification yet, calling Lucknow "one of India's greatest food cities" in a feature that traces the refinement of Awadhi cuisine from royal kitchens to roadside stalls. ## The Second City, After Hyderabad The UNESCO recognition, announced in October 2025 at the organization's General Conference in Samarkand, makes Lucknow only the second Indian city — after Hyderabad in 2019 — to join the global network of over 400 culinary cities. Tim Curtis, Director of UNESCO's Regional Office for South Asia, called it a testament to "deep-rooted culinary traditions and a vibrant food ecosystem." But for millions of NRIs who grew up with the smoky perfume of Tunday Kababi's 120-year-old kitchen in their memories, the recognition arrives less as news and more as long-overdue acknowledgment. ![Uttar Pradesh — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/1d/Taj_Mahal_%28Edited%29.jpeg) > **""The biggest misunderstanding is that Awadhi cuisine is 'heavy.' It isn't," Chef Ranveer Brar, the restaurateur and MasterChef India judge, told CNN."** ## A Cuisine Built on Restraint, Not Excess What sets Awadhi cuisine apart from the broader "Mughlai" label it is often lumped under is its emphasis on technique and restraint. Where Delhi's Mughlai cooking leans on bold gravies and assertive spice, Lucknow's kitchens operate on subtlety. "The biggest misunderstanding is that Awadhi cuisine is 'heavy.' It isn't," Chef Ranveer Brar, the restaurateur and MasterChef India judge, told CNN. "It is delicate. It is nuanced. It is built on restraint." The signature technique is *dum pukht* — slow cooking in a sealed pot, where steam is trapped, flavors develop gradually, and nothing is rushed. According to culinary lore, the method traces back to the late 18th century, when Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula fed famine laborers from large sealed pots during the construction of the Bara Imambara. The aromas reportedly drew the Nawab's own attention, and the technique was refined in royal kitchens from that point on. Then there are the kebabs. The galawati, made from finely minced meat and a closely guarded spice blend, is said to have been created for an aging Nawab who could no longer chew. The kakori, named after a nearby town, is shaped along skewers and charcoal-grilled. And the biryani — lighter and more aromatic than Hyderabad's famous version — layers separately cooked meat with rice and finishes under *dum*. ## Beyond the Famous Dishes What gets lost in the kebab-and-biryani narrative is Lucknow's extraordinary vegetarian tradition. From *desi ghee kachoris* to winter specialties like *kali gajar ka halwa* (black carrot pudding) and *malai makhan* (a cloud-like dessert of milk cream), the vegetarian repertoire is "seasonal, refined and deeply rooted in local traditions," says Atif Anzar, founder of Lucknow Heritage Walks. ![Nawabs of Awadh — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/10/Oudh-arms_short.gif) And then there's the city's famed chaat — the tangy, spicy, sweet street snacks that are a category of their own. *Aloo tikki*, *paani ke batashe*, *dahi bhalla* — each balanced with a precision that rivals the courtly dishes.
Awadhi Cuisine: A Study in Restraint
›Awadhi cuisine is known for its subtlety and technique.
›Signature cooking method: *dum pukht*, tracing back to the 18th century.
›Galawati kebabs created for a toothless Nawab.
›Biryani is lighter and more aromatic than Hyderabad's version.
## What It Means for the Diaspora For NRIs, Lucknow's recognition carries a particular weight. Many have spent years defending Indian cuisine against the global stereotype of "curry" — a catch-all that flattens thousands of regional traditions into a single, undifferentiated category. Lucknow's UNESCO designation is a crack in that wall. "We are at a time when authenticity matters again," says Chef Brar. "There is a global curiosity about origin stories — how food evolved and why it tastes the way it does. Awadhi cuisine represents sophistication without noise." Tourism is already responding. Anzar says that where once only a small number of visitors came specifically for Lucknow's food, most travelers now want curated food experiences — not just famous outlets but neighborhood spots and home dining. ## The Responsibility That Comes With Recognition
Culinary Tourism on the Rise
›Increased interest in curated food experiences in Lucknow.
›Travelers seek both famous outlets and local dining spots.
›Recognition encourages global curiosity about Indian food origins.
›Community initiatives needed to preserve traditional dishes.
Chef Sheeba Iqbal, who runs the home-dining experience Aab-o-Daana, sounds a note of caution. "Some hidden gems are fading away — dishes like *khichda*, *zarda* and *khameeri roti*," she says. "Community-led initiatives and food festivals can help bring these traditional dishes back to the forefront." For NRIs planning their next trip home, Lucknow just moved up the itinerary. But beyond tourism, the UNESCO designation is a signal: Indian cuisine's richest traditions are no longer content to stay local. They're going global — quietly, precisely, and on their own terms.
